turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mr Briggs is in the side room, Doctor. His daughter rang at opening — reckons he's fallen twice, and he's been dizzy.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mr Briggs, I'm Doctor Callahan. What happened at home?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): She doesn't ring the clinic for nothing.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Didn't fall.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. What did you do, if you didn't fall?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Slid twice, down to the floor. Kitchen, then the loo.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Down to the floor both times?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you black out?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or were you short of breath?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your daughter mentioned dizziness. Have you been woozy?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you first slide?

[SEG0017] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry to butt in. Lying was one fifty-two over eighty-six, pulse seventy-four — no, I misread it. Lying is one thirty-eight over eighty-two, pulse sixty-six, and standing after a minute was one oh four over sixty-four, pulse eighty-eight. He grabbed the bench and—
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Thursday. And yesterday.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thursday and yesterday. You grabbed the bench just now. Were you alright on your feet?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Woozy. Standing up.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll go with woozy when you stand. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0022] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): His daughter said the dizziness has been a fortnight. Both slides were this week, she told me. Chart's on the desk — I'm off.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): This week.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): This week from you, a fortnight from her. I'll note roughly one to two weeks, and leave it unsettled.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hit your head either time?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): The tablets are for your high blood pressure, yes?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which ones are you on?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Perindopril. Eight. Mornings.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Eight milligrams each morning. What else?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodipine. Five... no, ten.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ten milligrams, once a day?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other blood pressure tablet?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Little white one. Dunno.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): And a sleeping tablet?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Temazepam. Ten, maybe.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temazepam is usually every night. Are you taking it every night?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): So I'm not sure it's being taken the way it was prescribed. Ever had a heart trace?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Last winter. They said borderline.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just borderline, no figure. No bruise on the scalp or the arms. Heart sounds regular, no murmur. Chest is clear, and you swayed sitting to standing.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think the blood pressure is dropping when you stand, from the tablets. I can't rule out a rhythm problem with that old borderline trace, but the standing drop fits the tablets.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll reduce the amlodipine from ten milligrams to five, once a day. Keep perindopril at eight each morning. Leave the temazepam for when you need it, not every night. I won't change the white tablet until we know the name.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood test today for the kidneys and the salts. Get up slowly, and sit if you feel woozy. Come back in two weeks.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you slide again or you faint, come in sooner, or go up to emergency.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
